questions.a: The fraud model actively scores 98,912 of 112,400 accounts in scope. Of the 13,488 unscored, 11,240 are Howard University division accounts carried over from the merger and never mapped into the model's account master; the other 2,248 are recently opened and awaiting their first scoring cycle. suggested: Why did this get caught late?

questions.q: Why did this get caught late?
questions.a: Two reasons. The member authorizes the transfer themselves, so it looks legitimate to every control watching for unauthorized activity. And the signals sat in four systems — card, ACH, digital and core — each holding a fragment, so nobody was looking at the pattern. Mean time to detect is 2.4 days against a target under one.

Digital banking and ACH carry it: 69 and 50 of the 148 cases in the last 30 days, against 21 on card and 8 across branch and phone. Both of the growing channels are self-service, which is consistent with a pattern that works by convincing the member rather than by defeating a control.
followups: Why did this get caught late?

questions.a: From 18 cases a week eight weeks ago to 46 in the week ending Feb 8. Comparing the two 30-day windows: 148 against 94, a 57% rise. The slope steepened in the last two weeks, which is why this is a decision today rather than a watch item.

Nine receiving accounts repeat across 24 of the cases, and funds move on from them to five second-hop accounts — 14 flagged accounts in all. Repetition across otherwise unrelated victims is the signature: a one-off receiver is a case, a receiver appearing in four is a network.

Digital-banking alerts, ACH monitoring and member-services reports feed case management, which de-duplicates to one case per member per pattern. Every step is dated and every feed's last refresh is on the trust ribbon. That is the chain you can put in front of an examiner.

suggested: What is the exposure if nothing changes?

questions.q: What is the exposure if nothing changes?
questions.a: On the current slope, about 110 more cases over two weeks and roughly $148K of loss, at the current 71% pre-loss catch rate. Because these are authorized transfers, more of that lands on the member directly than on the credit union.

$148K baseline against $55K with the response. Most of it is the catch rate moving from 71% to 84% rather than the case count falling — the step-up catches transfers that would otherwise clear, which is a bigger lever than deterring the approach.

78% confidence, and the band on the chart is the honest range rather than decoration. It is a two-week horizon on eight weeks of observed slope; the further right you read, the wider the band. Treat the direction as solid and the point estimate as indicative.

Abrigo's published industry research puts a defrauded member at about 31% more likely to leave. That is a real figure, industry-wide across credit unions — ESFCU has never measured its own, and it is marked that way everywhere it appears. 61 members have carried a realized loss this year.

suggested: What does this mean for members?

questions.q: What does this mean for members?
questions.a: 61 members have carried a realized loss so far this year, and 31 are linked to the current campaign. Because they authorized the transfers, reimbursement is not automatic the way it is for unauthorized activity — which is exactly why the retention stake is higher here than the dollar figure suggests.

Every control we run asks whether the member made this transfer. Here they did — under a false pretext, but genuinely. So the transaction passes, recovery is far harder once funds move through a mule, and the member experiences it as the credit union having let it happen.
followups: What does this mean for members?

questions.a: ESFCU's published mission is fostering financial well-being for teachers and educators in Maryland — real and sourced from esfcu.org. Around 84,000 members across 13 Maryland branches plus the Howard University division, which merged in November 2024.

suggested: What is on the trust ribbon?

questions.q: What is on the trust ribbon?
questions.a: Four things, each with a state and a source: feed freshness (7 of 8 current), fraud-model coverage (88%, Howard University pending), open regulatory items (9 SARs, 2 due inside a week, 96% on-time), and NCUA and BSA exam readiness (81 of 100). Status is always a word plus an icon, never colour alone.

Composite across BSA programme documentation, SAR timeliness, fraud-model governance and lineage coverage. The open item dragging the score is fraud-model coverage — close the Howard University gap and it clears the ready threshold. Next window is Q4 2026.

questions.a: One thing: fraud-model coverage. 11,240 Howard University accounts are not scored, so any whole-book coverage claim is unsupported. It is flagged on the ribbon rather than averaged away, because a number you cannot defend to an examiner is worse than no number at all.

It is the only path that contains the campaign this week without charging the whole membership for it. The warning names the exact pattern, and the step-up is scoped to the transfer patterns the campaign uses — so the friction lands on the attack path. Modelled effect: $148K to $55K over two weeks.

It contains fastest and its loss reduction is comparable — the reason it is not recommended is the friction rating, not the containment. Every member making a legitimate transfer would feel it, and a lean fraud team would be clearing the manual-review backlog instead of working the real cases.

Because it is a two-week job and the campaign is running now — it does nothing for the next fourteen days. That is an argument for doing it alongside, not instead: the recommendation pairs option 1 with option 3 so the campaign is contained now and the blind spot is gone afterwards.

Member Communications and Digital Banking own the warning and the step-up, today. Fraud Operations and the BSA Officer own the holds and the two SAR filings, this week. Risk Technology and Data Governance own the coverage work, two weeks. Owners are roles rather than named individuals — the ESFCU risk roster is an open follow-up.

Two things. The targeted warning goes to the impacted segment in the language of the pattern in play, aligned to ESFCU's published fraud guidance so members are not getting two competing messages. And transfer step-up goes live on the flagged patterns — scoped, so the rest of the membership is untouched.

Nine are open against the 30-day clock; SAR-0412 and SAR-0409 fall due inside seven days and one of those is tied to the mule cluster, so its evidence is still being assembled. Both narratives are drafted with the lineage for every figure they cite — which is what makes them defensible to an examiner reading them cold.
